q.t: Who does the monarch invite to become Prime Minister?
q.e: The monarch invites the leader of the party with the largest number of MPs, or the leader of a coalition between more than one party, to become the Prime Minister.
o: The leader of the party with the largest number of MPs, or of a coalition
The leader of the second-largest party
The Speaker of the House of Commons
The longest-serving member of the House of Lords

q.t: Which THREE things may the monarch do in meetings with the Prime Minister?
q.e: The monarch has regular meetings with the Prime Minister and can advise, warn and encourage, but the decisions on government policies are made by the Prime Minister and cabinet.

q.t: What does the monarch do at the opening of the new parliamentary session each year?
q.e: The monarch has important ceremonial roles, such as the opening of the new parliamentary session each year. On this occasion the monarch makes a speech which summarises the government's policies for the year ahead.
o: Makes a speech summarising the government's policies for the year ahead
Appoints the Speaker of the House of Commons
Chooses the members of the cabinet
Announces the date of the next General Election

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
All Acts of Parliament are made in the monarch's name.
q.e: The monarch has important ceremonial roles, such as the opening of the new parliamentary session each year. All Acts of Parliament are made in the monarch's name.

q.t: What is the National Anthem of the UK?
q.e: The National Anthem of the UK is 'God Save the King (or Queen)'. It is played at important national occasions and at events attended by the King or Queen or the Royal Family.
o: I Vow to Thee, My Country

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: New citizens swear or affirm loyalty as part of the citizenship ceremony. The oath of allegiance begins 'I swear by Almighty God', while the affirmation of allegiance begins 'I do solemnly, sincerely and truly declare and affirm'.
o: New citizens may either swear an oath or make an affirmation of allegiance
New citizens must swear an oath by Almighty God with no alternative

q.t: About how many senior MPs does the Prime Minister appoint as ministers in charge of departments?
q.e: The Prime Minister appoints about 20 senior MPs to become ministers in charge of departments. These ministers form the cabinet, a committee which usually meets weekly and makes important decisions about government policy.

q.t: How often does the cabinet usually meet?
q.e: These ministers form the cabinet, a committee which usually meets weekly and makes important decisions about government policy. Many of these decisions have to be debated or approved by Parliament.

q.t: Which TWO junior ministerial roles exist in each government department?
q.e: Each department also has a number of other ministers, called Ministers of State and Parliamentary Under-Secretaries of State, who take charge of particular areas of the department's work.

q.t: What are the two official homes of the Prime Minister?
q.e: The official home of the Prime Minister is 10 Downing Street, in central London, near the Houses of Parliament. He or she also has a country house outside London called Chequers.
o: The Palace of Westminster and Chequers

q.t: Which party in the House of Commons is called the opposition?
q.e: The second-largest party in the House of Commons is called the opposition. The leader of the opposition usually becomes Prime Minister if his or her party wins the next General Election.
o: The party with the most MPs
Any party that is not in the cabinet
The party with the fewest MPs

q.t: How often does Prime Minister's Questions take place?
q.e: The leader of the opposition leads his or her party in pointing out what they see as the government's failures and weaknesses. One important opportunity to do this is at Prime Minister's Questions, which takes place every week while Parliament is sitting.
o: Every week while Parliament is sitting
Every day while Parliament is sitting

q.t: What is the role of the shadow cabinet?
q.e: The leader of the opposition also appoints senior opposition MPs to be 'shadow ministers'. They form the shadow cabinet and their role is to challenge the government and put forward alternative policies.
o: To challenge the government and put forward alternative policies
To advise the Prime Minister on policy
To chair debates in the House of Commons

q.t: What are MPs who do not represent any of the main political parties called?
q.e: There are a few MPs who do not represent any of the main political parties. They are called 'independents' and usually represent an issue important to their constituency.

q.t: Which TWO organisations are given as examples of pressure and lobby groups?
q.e: Pressure and lobby groups are organisations which try to influence government policy. Some are representative organisations such as the CBI, which represents the views of British business. Others campaign on particular topics, such as the environment, for example Greenpeace, or human rights, for example Liberty.

q.t: Which organisation represents the views of British business?
q.e: Some are representative organisations such as the CBI (Confederation of British Industry), which represents the views of British business.

q.t: Which TWO are core values of the civil service, according to the handbook?
q.e: Civil servants are expected to carry out their role with dedication and a commitment to the civil service and its core values. These are: integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality, including being politically neutral.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Civil servants are political appointees chosen by the governing party.
q.e: Civil servants support the government in developing and implementing its policies. Civil servants are accountable to ministers. They are chosen on merit and are politically neutral: they are not political appointees.

q.t: How are local authorities funded?
q.e: Towns, cities and rural areas in the UK are governed by democratically elected councils, often called 'local authorities'. Local authorities provide a range of services in their areas. They are funded by money from central government and by local taxes.
o: By money from central government and by local taxes

q.t: How many local authorities does London have, and what coordinates policies across the capital?
q.e: London has 33 local authorities, with the Greater London Authority and the Mayor of London coordinating policies across the capital.
o: 33 local authorities, coordinated by the Greater London Authority and the Mayor of London
60 local authorities, coordinated by the Greater London Authority
33 local authorities, coordinated by the Home Secretary
15 local authorities, coordinated by the Mayor of London

q.t: In which month are local elections for councillors usually held?
q.e: Many local authorities appoint a mayor, who is the ceremonial leader of the council. For most local authorities, local elections for councillors are held in May every year.

q.t: Since which year have powers been devolved from central government to Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland?
q.e: Since 1997, some powers have been devolved from the central government to give people in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland more control over matters that directly affect them. There has been a Welsh Assembly and a Scottish Parliament since 1999.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
The devolved administrations each have their own civil service.
q.e: Policy and laws governing defence, foreign affairs, immigration, taxation and social security all remain under central UK government control. However, many other public services, such as education, are controlled by the devolved administrations. The devolved administrations each have their own civil service.

q.t: Where does the Welsh Assembly meet?
q.e: In Wales the elected members, known as AMs, meet in the Welsh Assembly in the Senedd in Cardiff Bay.
